leading_positions.synthesis: Four of eight members include B024 (optical lattice clocks, Katori and Ye) in their round-1 configuration. Kroll and Lindroth propose it as the whole prize; Danielsson and Pearce make it one of two parts (see next position). All four describe it as a measurement-driven advance with independent reproduction at the 1e-18 level and a two-name credit. All four also record the same reservations, which are not resolved: overlap with the 2005 (frequency comb) and 2012 (single quantum systems) prizes, the pending redefinition of the second, and the unverified priority and credit tail (SYRTE, PTB, NIST and others). Kroll, Lindroth and Danielsson state that the performance figures and priority history rest on their own recollection.

Three members prefer B020 (twisted bilayer graphene; MacDonald, Bistritzer, Jarillo-Herrero) as the whole prize. They share the case of a quantitative prediction (Bistritzer-MacDonald, 2011) followed by an unexpected experimental discovery (2018) and wide independent reproduction. They also share the same reservations: an unresolved superconducting pairing mechanism, a field about eight years old, and the omission of Yuan Cao and earlier moire band-structure theorists. Eriksson and Olsson name B024 as a fallback alternative, and Mehlig also lists it as a third alternative after B051 (his own opening first choice, which he does not put in his configuration). Mehlig moved to B020 from B051 after reading the other ballots.

Two members prefer a two-part prize, B024 plus B019 (IceCube, credited to Francis Halzen alone), pairing a precision-measurement achievement with a discovery of a new observational window. They agree that the single-name Halzen credit is the weak point and that B019 should be the first part dropped if the credit cannot be defended, leaving B024 alone. They differ in what they would accept instead: Danielsson would consider a different second part, Pearce would not add names not supported by the shortlist. Neither has a settled view on whether the unresolved origin of most of the diffuse flux makes the discovery claim premature.

One member prefers B042 (circuit QED; Blais, Wallraff, Schoelkopf) as the whole prize and names B024 and B036 as alternatives. The same member discloses a field overlap and offers to accept a recusal ruling. The member also notes that Girvin is left out of the three-name credit and that the 2025 prize on superconducting circuits may make a second prize in the area too close. B042 appears as an alternative for Danielsson, Kroll, Lindroth and Pearce, but none of them includes it in their preferred configuration.

areas_of_agreement: B024 is the most widely supported ballot in the room: four of eight configurations include it, and B024 is a listed alternative for Eriksson, Johansson, Mehlig and Olsson (each of them has a different ballot in their own configuration, B020 or B042). Every member who comments on it regards its experimental results as solid and independently reproduced.
No member proposes more than three laureates in total, and every configuration is either a single ballot (B024, B020 or B042) or the two-part B024 plus B019.

Every member states a credit or maturity weakness in their own preferred configuration, and several say they would fall back to B024 (Eriksson and Olsson list it as an alternative; Danielsson and Pearce say B019 should be dropped first, leaving B024).

Several members say that the performance figures, priority histories and credit allocation they cite were taken from memory and should be checked against the record or an external expert report before a final ballot (Kroll, Lindroth, Danielsson, Mehlig).
scientific_disputes: Whether the optical lattice clock is a new discovery or a very good instrument in an already honoured lineage (2005 combs, 2012 single quantum systems). Kroll, Lindroth, Mehlig, Johansson and Pearce all raise this; Pearce and Kroll argue the lattice concept is distinct from both citations, while no member has shown this against the 2005 and 2012 citation texts.

Whether B020 is a settled enough discovery when the pairing mechanism of twisted bilayer graphene superconductivity is unresolved, and whether twist-angle disorder limits quantitative reproducibility. Supporters (Eriksson, Mehlig, Olsson) argue the phenomenology is secure and the citation can be worded around observed phases and the flat-band prediction; Pearce and Danielsson say they rely on colleagues for this field.

Whether IceCube's discovery claim is secure given that the origin of most of the diffuse flux is unsettled, versus the decade of consistent analyses, TXS 0506+056 and Galactic-plane associations cited by Danielsson and Pearce. Olsson ranked B019 eighth in the opening round and calls the Halzen credit fragile; nobody else comments on the physics beyond Danielsson, Pearce and Eriksson (who says he cannot judge from his own field).

Whether the committee prefers a thematically unified single-achievement prize or a split between unrelated areas (atomic metrology and neutrino astronomy), which Danielsson raises and Pearce says dilutes B024.
attribution_disputes: B019: Halzen alone is credited for a collaboration-scale result. AMANDA and IceCube builders, analysts and the collaboration are not named, and Danielsson, Pearce and Olsson all call this fragile. Danielsson notes there is room for two more names in a three-laureate prize, while Pearce says he cannot support extra names from the shortlist; no alternative credit is on the table.

B020: Yuan Cao (first author of the 2018 experiments) and earlier moire band-structure theorists (Lopes dos Santos, Peres, Castro Neto, Shallcross) are outside the three names (Eriksson, Mehlig, Olsson). The three supporters name the same trio, so the dispute is over whether the credit is sufficiently clean, not over who is credited.

B024: Katori and Ye are credited as proposer-and-first-demonstrator and record-performance group. Kroll and Lindroth note that SYRTE, PTB, NIST and others built much of the systematics programme, and Lindroth adds that Ye's credit rests partly on record accuracy and many-body clock physics rather than the original idea. Pearce and Kroll call this the cleanest credit on the shortlist, so members differ on how clean it is.
B042: Girvin is a central author of the 2004 proposal but is omitted by Johansson's trio, and Schoelkopf's contribution is broader than the first strong-coupling experiment.

B036 and B004 both involve Cirac and Zoller with different co-credited names (Blatt in B036; Bloch, Dalibard, Greiner in B004). No member prefers either, but Lindroth, Johansson, Mehlig and Pearce note that a partition between them is not clean.
maturity_disputes: B020: the field is about eight years old and the interpretation of the correlated phases is not fully stable (Eriksson, Mehlig, Olsson all list this as their main uncertainty).

B024: whether a prize should wait for the formal SI redefinition of the second (raised by Kroll, Lindroth, Pearce and Johansson), or whether the demonstrated performance and independent reproduction are sufficient now.
B019: about a decade of IceCube results, which Danielsson and Pearce regard as mature, against the unsettled origin of most of the diffuse flux.
B042: whether a second superconducting-circuit prize is too close to the 2025 prize (Johansson raises this against his own preference; Pearce says he cannot judge it in depth).
conflict_or_recusal_flags: Johansson directs the Wallenberg Centre for Quantum Technology, works on superconducting circuits and circuit QED, is a Chalmers MC2 colleague of Per Delsing and C. M. Wilson, and says Chalmers hosted the 2025 laureates; he disclosed a direct field overlap with B042 and says he would accept a recusal ruling. Olsson says she would support his recusal from deciding the attribution on B042.

Kroll disclosed a distant link to the Hall-Ye lineage: he spent a year in John Hall's laboratory during his PhD, and Jun Ye (credited in B024) trained in Hall's group. He reports no collaboration with Katori or Ye. Kroll also mentions his WACQT leadership role overlapping institutionally with Chalmers; this is relevant to B042, which is not in his preferred configuration.
Lindroth discloses a general interest and work in atomic precision physics, the field of B024; her close collaborators are not credited on any shortlisted ballot.
Pearce (chair) works in astroparticle physics (PAMELA, Fermi-LAT, XL-Calibur) and discloses field proximity to B019, with no stated connection to IceCube or Halzen.

Eriksson chaired the 2025 committee, which covered superconducting circuits, and says he should be mindful of this when weighing B042; he has no stated link to B020's credited names and says altermagnetism (B050, not shortlisted) is close to his own work.
Mehlig, Olsson and Johansson are in the Gothenburg/Chalmers environment; Mehlig describes this as institutional proximity without collaboration, and none of his preferred ballots involves Gothenburg.
Danielsson reports no specific conflict but flags that his voting status as a co-opted member and Secretary is not documented.
questions_for_round2: Can the committee defend Halzen as the sole credited laureate for B019? If not, should B019 be dropped from the two-part configuration, or does anyone propose a specific alternative credit (for example, additional named individuals or an instrument citation) that is supportable from the shortlist?

For B024 versus B020 as the whole prize: what evidence would B020 supporters need on the pairing mechanism, reproducibility and Yuan Cao's role to regard the field as mature, and what evidence would B024 supporters need on lineage and priority to regard it as distinct from the 2005 and 2012 prizes?

Do Eriksson, Mehlig and Olsson maintain B020 as the whole prize if B024 holds majority support, or would B024 be acceptable to them as a first part? Conversely, do Kroll and Lindroth see any pairing they could accept with B024?

Should the prize be a single thematically unified achievement or two distinct parts, and if two parts, what is the criterion for choosing the second part beyond B019 (for example B020, B042 or others)?

Should Johansson be recused from the B042 attribution discussion, and does B042 remain a live option given the 2025 prize on superconducting circuits? Does the committee want Girvin considered in place of one of the three names?

Is it acceptable to rely on members' recollection for the lattice-clock 1e-18 figures and priority history? Which specific claims (priority of the magic-wavelength proposal, clock-to-clock agreement, contributions of SYRTE, PTB, NIST) should be checked against the published record or an external expert report before the final ballot?
Should the committee wait for the formal redefinition of the second before recognising lattice clocks, and does this apply to the maturity standard used for the other candidates?
summary.chair_observation: Round 1 shows two substantial blocs and no consensus: four configurations include B024 (two as the whole prize, two paired with B019) and three prefer B020 alone, with one for B042. B024 is the common fallback of the B020 supporters, while no B024 supporter lists B020 as an alternative except Pearce, so the question is mainly whether B020 is mature and credited cleanly enough, and whether B019 can be given a defensible credit. The members have been transparent about reservations in their own configurations, and several would give up their own second or sole choice. The disclosed conflicts for Johansson and the field proximity of other members should be noted before round 2; no ruling is made here.
